# GA4 MCP Server — full text
Version 2.11.7, updated 2026-10-25. https://ga4mcp.com



# GA4 MCP client setup — the config each one expects
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-every-harness/


# Every client, and the config it actually wants

Most MCP installation guides give you one JSON block and tell you it works everywhere. It does not. Across the seventeen clients below there are six different root keys, four different names for the environment object, and four file formats.

Copying a Claude Desktop snippet into Hermes produces a file that parses and registers no servers. Copying one into OpenCode produces a server that never appears. Neither reports an error.

| What varies | Values across these clients |
|---|---|
| Root key | `mcpServers` (most clients), `servers` (VS Code), `context_servers` (Zed), `mcp` (OpenCode), `mcp_servers` (Hermes), `mcp.servers` (OpenClaw, ZCode) |
| Environment key | `env` (most), `envs` (Goose), `environment` (OpenCode), `env` plus `env_vars` (Codex) |
| Command shape | String everywhere except OpenCode, which takes an array |
| File format | JSON (most), TOML (Codex), YAML (Goose, Hermes, DeepSeek) |

Every block on the pages below is quoted from that vendor's own documentation, with the source page named. Where a vendor has not published a path, this site says so instead of inventing one.

<!--CLIENTS-->

## If your client is not here

It probably still works. The server speaks MCP over stdio, which is the transport every client here uses. Start from the shape used by the client closest to yours, run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal to confirm the server itself is fine, and then find where your client keeps its server list.

The server itself is client-agnostic. It speaks MCP over stdio. The only thing that changes per client is where the entry lives and what the surrounding keys are called.

## Next

Whichever client you pick, the credentials and verification steps are the same. Read [install](/setup/) for those, then [permissions](/iam/) when the first query returns a 403.



# Connect Antigravity IDE to GA4 (Setup & Queries)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-antigravity-ide/


# Connect Antigravity IDE to Google Analytics 4

The Antigravity IDE shares one MCP schema with the App and the CLI. Google's own documentation states it plainly: `mcp_config.json` follows a standardised schema, and the root object holds an `mcpServers` map.

What differs in the IDE is the management surface, not the file.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Once connected, run these directly in the IDE agent panel:

- **Site performance review**: "List top 10 pages by screenPageViews and average engagement time over the last 30 days."
- **Bot audit**: "Check sessions and bounceRate by city where bounceRate is 100% and session count exceeds 50."
- **AI referral tracking**: "Show sessions, totalUsers, and keyEvents referred by ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity this month."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup for the last 14 days."
- **Realtime visitors**: "Run a realtime report showing active users and top event names right now."

## The entry

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ga4": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## The two files

| Scope | Path |
|---|---|
| Global, every project | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` |
| This workspace | `<workspace>/.agents/mcp_config.json` |

The global path sits under `.gemini`, not a directory named after Antigravity. That surprises people who go looking for `~/.antigravity`.

## Managing it from the IDE

The IDE has a UI for the same file:

1. Open the agent side panel.
2. Click the `…` menu.
3. Choose **MCP Servers**.
4. Choose **Manage MCP Servers**.
5. Choose **View raw config** to see or edit the file.

That screen is the fastest way to find which of the two files is actually loaded, because it shows the resolved config rather than the one you think you edited.

> **Tip:** if you edit the workspace file and nothing changes, the global file probably wins for that project. Check the raw config view before assuming the entry was ignored.

## Remote servers are Streamable HTTP only

Worth knowing if you were planning to point the IDE at a hosted endpoint: it accepts Streamable HTTP with `serverUrl` (`url` also works). Legacy HTTP with SSE and `httpUrl` are explicitly unsupported.

This server is local stdio, so none of that applies — but it explains why a hosted Analytics MCP endpoint may or may not drop into the IDE depending on how it is served.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then check the MCP Servers list in the agent panel. A server that shows as installed with no tools means the process exited after launching; run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal to see the error.

## Next

[Antigravity App and CLI](/ga4-mcp-for-antigravity/) for the other two surfaces, [install](/setup/) for the credentials.



# Connect Google Antigravity to GA4 (App, IDE & CLI)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-antigravity/


# Connect Google Antigravity to Google Analytics 4

Antigravity ships as an app, an IDE and a CLI, and all three use the same `mcp_config.json` schema and the same two file paths. What differs is only how you get the entry in.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Once connected, ask Antigravity:

- **Weekly health check**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days against the previous 7 days."
- **AI referral audit**: "Check sessions and keyEvents from chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and perplexity.ai over the last 30 days."
- **Drop-off triage**: "Identify our top 5 pages by screenPageViews that have an engagementRate below 40% over the last 30 days."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Show sessions, keyEvents, and userEngagementDuration by sessionDefaultChannelGroup for this month."
- **Live traffic check**: "Run a realtime report showing active users and top pages over the last 30 minutes."

## App and IDE: use the settings UI

In the Antigravity app, servers are added through **Settings → Customizations → Installed MCP Servers**. That flow writes the config for you, which is the safer route because Antigravity does not publish an absolute path for the file on every platform.

Paste the entry below into that UI.

## The entry

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The root key is `mcpServers`, the same as Claude Desktop, Cursor and Gemini CLI. `env` sits inside the server object.

## Where the file lives

Two paths, both shared across the App, the IDE and the CLI:

| Scope | Path |
|---|---|
| Global, every project | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` |
| This workspace | `<workspace>/.agents/mcp_config.json` |

The global path sits under `.gemini`, not a directory named after Antigravity. If you went looking for `~/.antigravity` and found nothing, that is why.

The settings screen writes one of these two files. Editing the file by hand works equally well, and the [IDE guide](/ga4-mcp-for-antigravity-ide/) shows where the IDE exposes the raw config.

## Verify

In the agent panel:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then confirm the server shows as connected in the MCP servers list under Customizations. A server that appears but exposes no tools usually means the process launched and exited — run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal to see why.

## Using the CLI surface

The CLI reads the same schema. Because the client is Google's own, an alternative worth knowing: Google publishes a hosted Analytics MCP endpoint at `analyticsdata.googleapis.com/mcp/v1` that needs no local process at all. It exposes reporting and metadata tools and nothing else. Use it if you want zero install; use this server when you want the skill layer and the setup recovery.

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for the two values, [permissions](/iam/) when the first query returns a 403.



# Connect Claude to Google Analytics 4 (Code & Desktop)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-claude/


# Connect Claude to Google Analytics 4

Claude has two surfaces that run local MCP servers, and they take different configuration. Claude Code is a CLI and registers the server from your terminal. Claude Desktop reads a JSON file.

## Prerequisites

You need the numeric property ID and either a service-account key path or a `gcloud` login. Both are covered in [install](/setup/). Keep the key path absolute.

## Claude Code

One command:

```bash
claude mcp add google-analytics -- uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

The `--` matters. Everything after it is passed to the server untouched, so a future flag on the server is not swallowed by the CLI parser.

To pass the two environment variables at registration time instead of exporting them:

```bash
claude mcp add --env GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 --env GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json --transport stdio google-analytics -- uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

If you would rather hand it a full entry as JSON:

```bash
claude mcp add-json google-analytics '{"type":"stdio","command":"uvx","args":["google-analytics-mcp"],"env":{"GA4_PROPERTY_ID":"123456789","GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS":"/absolute/path/to/key.json"}}'
```

Claude Code stores project-scoped servers in `.mcp.json` at the repository root, and user-scoped ones in `~/.claude.json`. Either is fine; project scope is the better default for a server that belongs to one analytics property.

## Claude Desktop

Open the config file. On macOS it is here:

```text
~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
```

On Windows it is `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`. You can also reach it from the app: **Settings → Developer → Edit Config**.

Add the entry:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Save, then quit Claude Desktop completely and reopen it. A window close is not a restart; the server list is read at launch.

## Verify

Ask this in either surface:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Success is `list_properties` returning rows with no setup error. An empty list means the credentials work but the service account has access to no properties — see [permissions](/iam/).

## Five questions you can ask Claude once connected

Once connected, Claude has direct access to the Google Analytics Data API with server-side totals and schema verification:

1. **Executive acquisition summary**:
   ```text
   Summarize our top 5 acquisition channels by sessions over the last 30 days. Report sessions, active users, and key event conversions.
   ```
2. **AI search traffic analysis**:
   ```text
   Show all traffic arriving from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 90 days. What is the month-over-month growth rate?
   ```
3. **Traffic drop investigation**:
   ```text
   Our organic traffic dropped this week compared to last week. Follow the traffic-diagnosis methodology to isolate which channel and pages dropped first.
   ```
4. **Landing page bounce audit**:
   ```text
   Which top landing pages have a bounce rate over 60% with at least 150 sessions this month?
   ```
5. **E-commerce funnel conversion**:
   ```text
   What was our overall checkout-to-purchase conversion rate across the last 60 days? Break down purchase revenue by channel.
   ```

## The two failures specific to Claude

**The server does not appear in Claude Code.** Run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` on its own in a terminal. If that fails, the CLI is not the problem and no amount of re-registering will fix it. Usually `uv` is missing from the PATH that the client inherits.

**Claude Desktop shows a setup error on launch.** The `env` block is outside the server object, or the credentials path is relative. Both variables must sit inside the same object as `command`, and the path must start with `/` on macOS or a drive letter on Windows.

> **Note:** the installer at `/setup/` writes both entries for you, which avoids the JSON entirely.

## Next

[Skills](/skills/) explains what to load before asking an analytical question. [Query shapes](/schema/) covers filter syntax, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) provides 35 tested templates.



# Connect OpenAI Codex to Google Analytics 4 (Data API)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-codex/


# Connect OpenAI Codex to Google Analytics 4

Codex is the one client in this set that configures MCP servers in TOML rather than JSON, and the one that splits environment handling into two separate keys. Both trip people up.

## One command

```bash
codex mcp add google-analytics --env GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 --env GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json -- uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

As with Claude Code, the `--` separates Codex's own flags from the command it will launch.

## The file

Codex reads `~/.codex/config.toml` for every session, and `.codex/config.toml` inside a project that Codex has been told to trust. Project config only applies to trusted projects, which is a deliberate security boundary rather than a bug.

```toml
[mcp_servers.google-analytics]
command = "uvx"
args = ["google-analytics-mcp"]

[mcp_servers.google-analytics.env]
GA4_PROPERTY_ID = "123456789"
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS = "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
```

That is the whole entry. TOML table headers do the work that JSON braces do elsewhere.

## env versus env_vars

This is the part that catches people, and it is specific to Codex.

- `env` **sets** a value. Use it when you want to write the value in the file.
- `env_vars` **allows an existing environment variable through** to the server. Use it when the value lives in your shell or a secret manager and you do not want it in the file.

So these two entries do different things:

```toml
[mcp_servers.google-analytics.env]
GA4_PROPERTY_ID = "123456789"
```

```toml
[mcp_servers.google-analytics]
env_vars = ["GA4_PROPERTY_ID", "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"]
```

The first hardcodes the property ID. The second forwards whatever the shell has. Both are valid; putting a bare value inside `env_vars` is not, because that key takes names and not assignments.

A common arrangement is a hardcoded property ID plus a forwarded credentials path:

```toml
[mcp_servers.google-analytics]
command = "uvx"
args = ["google-analytics-mcp"]
env_vars = ["GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"]

[mcp_servers.google-analytics.env]
GA4_PROPERTY_ID = "123456789"
```

## Verify

Start Codex and ask:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then check that the tool appears in Codex's MCP list. If the entry loads but every call fails with a setup error, one of the two variables is missing — the TOML parsed, the `env` table did not apply.

## Five questions you can ask Codex CLI

Once registered, you can query your analytics directly in your terminal:

1. **Traffic overview**:
   ```text
   What were our top 10 landing pages by sessions over the last 30 days?
   ```
2. **Channel performance**:
   ```text
   Compare sessions, engagement rate, and bounce rate across our top 5 acquisition channels.
   ```
3. **AI search citations**:
   ```text
   How much referral traffic did we receive from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 60 days?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Analyze our traffic drop over the last 14 days compared to the prior period. Which channel fell first?
   ```
5. **E-commerce metrics**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and conversion rate by country for the past 30 days?
   ```

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [permissions](/iam/) for the 403 that means the service account is not on the property yet, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) for 35 tested templates.



# Connect Cursor to Google Analytics 4 (Setup & Queries)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-cursor/


# Connect Cursor to Google Analytics 4

Cursor reads MCP servers from a JSON configuration file and supports an environment object per server. Setup is one entry and a window reload.

## Where the file lives

Cursor accepts two locations:

- **Project:** `.cursor/mcp.json` in the repository root. Committed with the project, shared with anyone who clones it.
- **Global:** `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Applies to every workspace on the machine.

Use the project file when the server is tied to one analytics property. Use the global file when you want GA4 available everywhere and you accept that the credentials path is machine-specific.

## The entry

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Save the file. Cursor picks up changes to the MCP config without a full restart, but the first registration needs one — reload the window from the command palette (**Cmd+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window**).

## About the type field

Cursor's configuration reference marks `type` as a required field on stdio servers, with the value `"stdio"`. Every copy-paste example on the same page omits it.

In practice the field is optional and Cursor infers stdio when `command` is present. If the server does not appear, add it explicitly:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

That is the shape the reference documents, and it is the one to prefer when something is not working.

## Keeping secrets out of the file

Cursor also supports `envFile`, which reads variables from a dotenv file instead of inlining them. That keeps the credentials path out of a committed `.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "envFile": ".env.local"
    }
  }
}
```

With `GA4_PROPERTY_ID` and `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` set in `.env.local`, which stays out of version control.

## Verify

In Cursor's chat or Composer panel:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

If the tool list is empty, the file did not parse. Cursor silently ignores a malformed `mcp.json` rather than reporting an error, so validate the JSON before assuming the server is at fault.

## Five questions you can ask Cursor once connected

Once Cursor recognizes the `@google-analytics` tools, you can query your analytics directly while coding:

1. **Traffic overview**:
   ```text
   What were our top 10 landing pages by sessions over the last 30 days? Show activeUsers and engagementRate.
   ```
2. **Channel breakdown**:
   ```text
   Break down our acquisition channels for the past 60 days. Which channel drove the highest average engagement time?
   ```
3. **AI referral tracking**:
   ```text
   How many sessions arrived from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity this month?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Diagnose why organic search traffic dropped between last week and this week. Which landing pages were most affected?
   ```
5. **E-commerce & revenue**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and average order value (AOV) for the last 30 days grouped by country?
   ```

## Next

[Install](/setup/) covers credentials, [permissions](/iam/) covers the 403 you will hit if the service account was never added to the property, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) provides 35 tested analytical recipes.



# Connect DeepSeek Harness to GA4 (Data API Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-deepseek/


# Connect DeepSeek Harness to Google Analytics 4

DeepSeek Harness mounts MCP servers as config entries in its composed tree, not through a settings screen. One entry in your patch layer adds the server, and its tools appear inside the session.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Ask DeepSeek Harness inside your session:

- **Weekly traffic diagnosis**: "Compare activeUsers and sessions between this week and last week. Identify top 3 traffic sources by drop or gain."
- **AI referral report**: "Report all sessions, bounceRate, and keyEvents from chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and perplexity.ai in the last 30 days."
- **Page engagement check**: "Fetch top 10 pages by screenPageViews and userEngagementDuration for the last 14 days."
- **Conversion funnel audit**: "Query sessions, keyEvents, and sessionConversionRate grouped by sessionDefaultChannelGroup."
- **Live traffic snapshot**: "Run a realtime report to see active visitors and active pages right now."

## The entry

Add this to your patch layer:

```yaml
- id: mcp-ga4
  name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client'
  config:
    serverName: ga4
    transport: stdio
    command: uvx
    args: ['google-analytics-mcp']
    env:
      GA4_PROPERTY_ID: '123456789'
      GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS: '/absolute/path/to/key.json'
```

The package is `@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client`, scoped. There is an unscoped `dsh-mcp-client` on npm published by someone else as a name reservation — it is not the DeepSeek client and installing it gives you nothing.

## Where the patch goes

`DSH_HOME` defaults to `~/.dsh`. Two patch files are read, in this order:

- `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` applies to every profile
- `$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml` applies to one

An explicit `--patch` overlay wins over both. If you only run one profile, the first file is the simplest place.

## Reading environment from the shell

The `env` block takes literals, and DeepSeek's config supports a JavaScript tag if you would rather not write the path into the file:

```yaml
    env:
      GA4_PROPERTY_ID: '123456789'
      GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS: !!js process.env.GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
```

That keeps the credentials path out of a file you might commit. The property ID stays literal; it is not a secret.

## Tool names inside the session

Tools surface as `mcp__<serverName>__<tool>`. With `serverName: ga4` above, the agent sees:

```text
mcp__ga4__get_ga4_data
mcp__ga4__search_schema
mcp__ga4__list_properties
```

If you mount two properties, give them different `serverName` values and the tool lists stay separable.

## Verify

Check the composed config first, before you start a session:

```bash
dsh web --dump-config
```

The `mcp-ga4` entry and its resolved `env` should appear in the output. Then ask:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [query shapes](/schema/) when a call fails on a filter rather than credentials.



# Connect Devin Desktop (Windsurf) to GA4 MCP
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-devin-desktop/


# Connect Devin Desktop (Windsurf) to GA4 MCP

Devin Desktop is the current name for Windsurf. The rename happened on 2 June 2026, so older guides and forum answers still call it Windsurf. The config schema did not change with the name.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

In Cascade chat, try asking:

- **Weekly health check**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days with the previous 7 days."
- **AI referral traffic**: "Show sessions, keyEvents, and userEngagementDuration from chatgpt.com and perplexity.ai in the last 30 days."
- **Bounce rate audit**: "Find top 10 landing pages by sessions where bounceRate is above 60% over the last 30 days."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Query sessions and keyEvents grouped by sessionDefaultChannelGroup for the last 14 days."
- **Realtime active visitors**: "Run a realtime report showing active users and top pages right now."

## The entry

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Root key `mcpServers`, standard `env` object. Nothing unusual in the shape.

## The path problem, stated plainly

Devin's own documentation gives two different paths for the same file, and both pages are live today:

- The Cascade MCP page says `~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json` on macOS and Linux, and `%APPDATA%\devin\mcp_config.json` on Windows.
- The Devin Desktop FAQ says the MCP config is `~/.codeium/mcp_config.json`, and adds that the `~/.codeium/` directory structure is not changing in this release.

Rather than pick one and hope, check which file exists on your machine:

```bash
ls -la ~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json ~/.codeium/mcp_config.json
```

Edit whichever one is present. If neither exists, create the `.config/devin` one and restart the app — the newer path is the one on the MCP page.

> **Note:** if you are migrating from Windsurf and MCP servers still work, you are on the `.codeium` path and can leave it alone. The rename did not move it.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then open the MCP panel in Cascade and confirm the server is running. Devin shows a failed launch there, which distinguishes a bad config from a bad credential — a distinction the other clients here generally do not make.

## If you are on Windsurf

Windsurf, before the rename, used the same `mcpServers` shape. Older Windsurf documentation and this page are compatible; only the file path differs by app version.

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for the two values, [skills](/skills/) for what to load before asking a question that needs interpretation.



# Connect Gemini CLI to Google Analytics 4 (Data API)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-gemini/


# Connect Gemini CLI to Google Analytics 4

Gemini CLI reads MCP servers from a `settings.json` file and can also register them from the command line. The one behaviour worth knowing before you start: the default scope is **project**, not user.

## One command

```bash
gemini mcp add -e GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 -e GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json google-analytics uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

The shape is `gemini mcp add [options] <name> <command> [args...]`, so the server name comes before the command and anything after it becomes an argument to the server.

Add `--scope user` if you want the entry in your home directory instead of the current project:

```bash
gemini mcp add --scope user -e GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 -e GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json google-analytics uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

Without that flag the entry goes to `.gemini/settings.json` inside the directory you ran it from. That is the single most common surprise: it works in one repository and appears missing in the next.

## The file

User scope is `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Project scope is `.gemini/settings.json`.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The root key is `mcpServers`, which matches Claude Desktop and Cursor. Gemini additionally accepts three optional keys on a stdio server that the others do not:

- `cwd` — working directory for the spawned process
- `timeout` — milliseconds before the client gives up on a call
- `trust` — skip the confirmation prompt for tool calls

For a read-only analytics server, `"trust": true` removes a confirmation click per query and changes nothing about what the server can do.

## A project-scoped example

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      },
      "trust": true,
      "timeout": 30000
    }
  }
}
```

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

If Gemini reports no GA4 tools, check the scope before anything else. Run `gemini mcp list` and confirm which file the entry actually landed in.

## Five questions you can ask Gemini CLI

Once registered, you can query your Google Analytics data from your terminal:

1. **Traffic overview**:
   ```text
   What were our top 5 acquisition channels by sessions over the last 30 days?
   ```
2. **AI search citations**:
   ```text
   Show all traffic arriving from AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity) for the past 60 days.
   ```
3. **Engagement audit**:
   ```text
   Which 10 landing pages had the highest average engagement time among organic search visitors?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Compare this week's active users with last week's. Did organic or direct traffic drive the variance?
   ```
5. **E-commerce breakdown**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and average order value across the last 30 days?
   ```

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for credentials, [skills](/skills/) for the recipes the agent can load once it is connected, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) for 35 tested templates.



# Connect Goose CLI to Google Analytics 4 (MCP Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-goose/


# Connect Goose CLI to Google Analytics 4

Goose is the only client here that configures MCP servers in YAML, and it renames two fields you would otherwise expect. `cmd` instead of `command`, `envs` instead of `env`.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Inside your Goose session, run:

- **Weekly health check**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days against the previous 7 days."
- **AI referral audit**: "Fetch sessions and keyEvents from chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and perplexity.ai over the last 30 days."
- **Top content performance**: "Show top 10 landing pages by screenPageViews and average engagement time for the last 30 days."
- **Acquisition breakdown**: "Break down sessions, activeUsers, and bounceRate by sessionDefaultChannelGroup."
- **Realtime traffic**: "Run a realtime report for active visitors and current page views."

## The file

`~/.config/goose/config.yaml`

Add an `extensions` block. If the file already has one, add the server under it rather than creating a second `extensions` key.

```yaml
extensions:
  google-analytics:
    name: Google Analytics
    cmd: uvx
    args: [google-analytics-mcp]
    enabled: true
    envs:
      GA4_PROPERTY_ID: "123456789"
      GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS: "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
    type: stdio
```

Every one of the five keys matters:

- `cmd` — the executable. `command` is silently ignored.
- `args` — a YAML flow sequence, so it stays on one line in brackets.
- `envs` — plural. `env` is silently ignored, and the server starts without credentials and fails at the first query.
- `type` — `stdio` for a local process.
- `enabled` — Goose writes `false` here when you disable an extension, and the server will not launch.

## One-off without the file

For a single session, Goose takes the command inline:

```bash
goose session --with-extension "GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json uvx google-analytics-mcp"
```

That form passes the environment through the shell rather than YAML, which makes it the fastest way to confirm the server works before you edit a config file.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then check the extension list. Goose reports a broken extension on startup, which makes it friendlier than most clients here — you get an error instead of silence.

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for the two values, [permissions](/iam/) when the first query returns a 403 rather than a setup error.



# Connect Hermes Agent to Google Analytics 4 (MCP Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-hermes/


# Connect Hermes Agent to Google Analytics 4

Hermes is Nous Research's agent harness. It configures MCP servers in YAML, and the root key is `mcp_servers` — snake case. A Claude Desktop snippet pasted here produces a file that parses fine and registers nothing.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Inside Hermes Agent:

- **Weekly performance overview**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate for the last 7 days against the previous period."
- **AI referral audit**: "Show me sessions, bounceRate, and keyEvents referred by ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 30 days."
- **High-bounce page check**: "List top 10 pages by sessions where bounceRate exceeds 60% over the last 30 days."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup this month."
- **Realtime traffic status**: "Run a realtime report showing active users and top pages over the last 30 minutes."

## The entry

In `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  ga4:
    command: "uvx"
    args: ["google-analytics-mcp"]
```

That is the shape Hermes documents. Note the two differences from the common JSON form: the root key is `mcp_servers`, and the file is YAML, so indentation carries the structure.

## Credentials

Hermes' documented example shows `command` and `args` only. It does not publish an environment key for this block, and this server cannot run without two values.

The reliable route is to export them before launching Hermes, so the server process inherits them:

```bash
export GA4_PROPERTY_ID="123456789"
export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="/absolute/path/to/key.json"
```

Launch Hermes from that shell. Application default credentials work here too — run `gcloud auth application-default login` once and you can drop the second variable.

> **Note:** if a future Hermes release documents an `env` key, prefer it over shell inheritance. This page states shell export because that is what the vendor documents today.

## Migrating from Claude

Hermes ships a migration command that rewrites a Claude configuration into its own shape:

```bash
hermes import-agent claude-code
```

It maps Claude's `mcpServers` in `~/.claude.json` onto `mcp_servers` in `config.yaml`. Worth running even if you only want the shape as a reference — the output shows exactly how Hermes expects a server to look.

There is also a picker and a catalog:

```bash
hermes mcp
```

```bash
hermes mcp install ga4
```

The catalog holds entries from Hermes' own `optional-mcps` directory. If GA4 is not in it, the manual block above is the path.

## Do not confuse the packages

`hermes-mcp` on PyPI is the opposite direction: an MCP server that exposes a Hermes agent to other clients. Installing it does not give Hermes access to Analytics.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

If the agent has no GA4 tools at all, check the root key first. `mcpServers` in that file is valid YAML and completely inert.

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [query shapes](/schema/) when a query fails on a filter.



# Connect Kiro IDE to Google Analytics 4 (MCP Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-kiro/


# Connect Kiro IDE to Google Analytics 4

Kiro reads MCP servers from `mcp.json` and reloads the file the moment you save it. That is the main practical difference from the rest of this set — you will not be restarting the editor.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Ask Kiro directly in the chat panel:

- **Weekly performance overview**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days against the previous 7 days."
- **AI referral audit**: "Show me sessions, bounceRate, and keyEvents from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 30 days."
- **Content drop-off triage**: "List top 10 pages by screenPageViews where engagementRate is below 40%."
- **Acquisition channels**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup for the last 14 days."
- **Realtime traffic check**: "Run a realtime report showing active users and top pages over the last 30 minutes."

## Where the file lives

- **Workspace:** `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` inside the project.
- **User:** `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`, applied everywhere.

Workspace scope wins when both exist.

## The entry

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      },
      "disabled": false,
      "autoApprove": ["list_properties", "search_schema", "get_ga4_data"]
    }
  }
}
```

The root key is `mcpServers`. The three optional keys are Kiro-specific:

- `disabled` — set `true` to keep the entry but stop it launching.
- `autoApprove` — tool names that run without a confirmation prompt. For a read-only analytics server there is no reason to confirm each call.
- `disabledTools` — the inverse. Useful for hiding `check_for_updates` or `setup_ga4_access` from an agent you want focused on reporting.

Kiro also expands environment placeholders, so a credentials path can come from the shell:

```json
"env": {
  "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
  "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS}"
}
```

## From the CLI

```bash
kiro-cli mcp add --name google-analytics --scope global --command uvx --args google-analytics-mcp --env GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789
```

`--args` takes one argument per flag, so a server with several arguments needs the flag repeated rather than a single space-separated string.

## Verify

Save the file, then ask:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

The server should appear without a restart. If it does not, check the MCP servers panel — Kiro reports a launch failure there rather than failing silently, which it can do because it is watching the process rather than reading a file once.

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for the two values, [permissions](/iam/) for the 403 that means the service account is not on the property.



# Connect OpenClaw to Google Analytics 4 (MCP Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-openclaw/


# Connect OpenClaw to Google Analytics 4

OpenClaw is an MCP client directly, so the server needs no plugin. One command writes the entry.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Inside OpenClaw, try:

- **Weekly performance overview**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days against the previous 7 days."
- **AI referral audit**: "Show sessions and keyEvents from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 30 days."
- **Landing page triage**: "List top 10 pages by sessions where bounceRate is higher than 60%."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup this month."
- **Realtime traffic snapshot**: "Run a realtime report for active users and top pages over the last 30 minutes."

## Add the server

```bash
openclaw mcp add ga4 --command uvx --arg google-analytics-mcp
```

`--arg` repeats once per server argument. That writes an entry under `mcp.servers` in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "ga4": {
        "command": "uvx",
        "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
        "env": {
          "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
          "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Edit the file to add the two `env` values — the server will not start usefully without them. The root key is `mcp.servers`, two levels deep, not `mcpServers` at the top.

## Check it launched

```bash
openclaw mcp doctor ga4 --probe
```

`--probe` is the part that matters. Without it you get configuration validation; with it, OpenClaw actually starts the process and reports whether the handshake completes. A server that configures cleanly and fails the probe is almost always a missing environment variable.

## Where the file lives

`~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`. OpenClaw also discovers plugins from configured paths, workspace roots and global plugin roots, but MCP servers are separate from plugins and live in this one file.

## About the plugin route

The repository ships a file at `plugins/openclaw/plugin.json`. It is not an installable OpenClaw manifest. OpenClaw's documented manifest is `openclaw.plugin.json`, and its required fields are `id` and `configSchema` — neither of which that file has.

Use `openclaw mcp add` above. A plugin is only worth building if you want to distribute a bundle; a single local server does not need one.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

If `doctor` reports the server running and the tools still do not appear in a session, the property ID is wrong rather than the config. Read [install](/setup/) for the difference between the property ID and the measurement ID.

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for credentials, [skills](/skills/) for the recipes the agent can load once connected.



# Connect OpenCode to Google Analytics 4 (Local stdio)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-opencode/


# Connect OpenCode to Google Analytics 4

OpenCode's MCP config is the furthest from the Claude Desktop baseline in this whole set. Four things are named differently, and a standard snippet will not load.

## The entry

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["uvx", "google-analytics-mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "environment": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Read the four differences carefully, because each one fails silently:

| Elsewhere | OpenCode |
|---|---|
| `mcpServers` | `mcp` |
| `"type": "stdio"` | `"type": "local"` |
| `"command": "uvx"` plus a separate `args` array | one `command` array holding the executable and its arguments |
| `env` | `environment` |

There is no `args` key. The executable and every argument live in the same array.

## Where the file lives

- **Global:** `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
- **Project:** `opencode.json` in the working directory

Both accept JSON or JSONC. A project file takes precedence over the global one.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then confirm the server appears in OpenCode's MCP list. If it does not, check the `type` value first — `"stdio"` is valid everywhere else and invalid here.

## A note on multiple properties

OpenCode's project-scoped config makes it easy to run one entry per property, which is useful if you work across several sites. Each entry gets its own key and its own `GA4_PROPERTY_ID`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "ga4-studio": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["uvx", "google-analytics-mcp"],
      "environment": { "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "111111111", "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/keys/studio.json" }
    },
    "ga4-client": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["uvx", "google-analytics-mcp"],
      "environment": { "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "222222222", "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/keys/client.json" }
    }
  }
}
```

The agent then sees two servers with the same tools and different data, which is usually clearer than one server whose property changes between sessions.

## Five questions you can ask in OpenCode

Once registered, you can ask OpenCode directly during agentic sessions:

1. **Traffic overview**:
   ```text
   What were our top 10 landing pages by sessions over the last 30 days?
   ```
2. **Channel performance**:
   ```text
   Compare sessions, engagement rate, and bounce rate across our acquisition channels for the past 60 days.
   ```
3. **AI referral tracking**:
   ```text
   How many sessions arrived from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity this month?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Diagnose why organic search traffic dropped between last week and this week. Which landing pages were most affected?
   ```
5. **E-commerce & revenue**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and average order value (AOV) for the last 30 days grouped by country?
   ```

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for the two values, [permissions](/iam/) when the first query returns a 403, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) for 35 tested templates.



# Connect Pi Agent to Google Analytics 4 (MCP Setup)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-pi/


# Connect Pi Agent to Google Analytics 4

Pi reads MCP servers from a JSON file beside its agent configuration, and also takes them from the command line. Two files matter, and the project one only counts after you trust the project.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Inside Pi session:

- **Weekly health check**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days with the prior period."
- **AI referral audit**: "Show sessions, keyEvents, and userEngagementDuration from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 30 days."
- **Landing page check**: "List top 10 pages by sessions where bounceRate is above 60% over the last 30 days."
- **Acquisition channels**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup this month."
- **Realtime traffic check**: "Run a realtime report for active users and top pages right now."

## The entry

In your agent directory's `mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ga4": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Two locations, matching Pi's own wording of `<agent-dir>/mcp.json`:

| Scope | Path |
|---|---|
| User | `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` |
| Project | `.pi/mcp.json` in the project root |

The project file is only read once Pi trusts that project. If the server works in one repository and not another, trust is the reason.

## From the command line

```bash
pi mcp add ga4 --command uvx --arg google-analytics-mcp --env GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 --env GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json
```

`pi mcp` also lists and removes servers. Note that `--arg` repeats once per argument rather than taking a single string.

> **Note:** there is no `/codemcp` command and no `pi-mcp` package. An earlier version of this page named both; neither exists. The interactive command is `/mcp`, and `codemode` is a tool-exposure mode rather than a slash command.

## Managing at runtime

Inside a Pi session, `/mcp` is the interactive surface: inspect connected servers, reconnect one, change how its tools are exposed, or disable it for the session.

That is the fastest way to check whether the entry loaded at all. A server listed with zero tools means the process launched and exited — run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal to see why.

## Tool names

Pi prefixes MCP tools as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, so with the server named `ga4` above the agent calls `mcp__ga4__get_ga4_data`. Naming the server `ga4` rather than `google-analytics` keeps the tool names short enough to read in a transcript.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then `/mcp` to confirm the server is connected rather than merely configured.

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [skills](/skills/) for what to load before an analytical question.



# Connect VS Code & Copilot to Google Analytics 4
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-vscode/


# Connect VS Code & Copilot to Google Analytics 4

VS Code's agent mode runs MCP servers, and the configuration has one trap that catches almost everyone: the root key depends on which file you are editing.

## Pick the right file first

| File | Root key | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| `.vscode/mcp.json` | `servers` | This workspace |
| `.mcp.json` at the workspace root | `mcpServers` | This workspace, portable shape |
| `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` | `mcpServers` | Every workspace for this user |

The two workspace files are not interchangeable. A config that works in one is silently ignored in the other, because the top-level key does not match what that file expects. This is the single most common reason a working snippet "does nothing" in VS Code.

## The workspace entry

In `.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Note `servers`, and note that `type` is required here.

## The portable entry

In `.mcp.json` at the workspace root:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Use this one if you want the same file to work in other clients that read `.mcp.json`.

## The CLI route

One command, no file editing:

```bash
code --add-mcp '{"name":"google-analytics","type":"stdio","command":"uvx","args":["google-analytics-mcp"],"env":{"GA4_PROPERTY_ID":"123456789","GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS":"/absolute/path/to/key.json"}}'
```

Note that the CLI object uses `name` rather than a keyed object — it is a different shape from the file, not a copy of it.

## Environment variable substitution

`.vscode/mcp.json` can read values from your environment instead of hardcoding a credentials path:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "${env:GA4_PROPERTY_ID}",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "${env:GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS}"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The `${env:NAME}` form is specific to `.vscode/mcp.json`. The portable `.mcp.json` uses `${NAME}` instead. Another reason not to move a block between the two files.

## If you use Cline or Roo Code

Those are extensions with their own MCP settings, not consumers of `.vscode/mcp.json`. The installer writes their entries separately, so the fastest path is:

```bash
curl -fsSL "https://ga4.builditwithai.xyz/install" | bash
```

## Verify

Open the Copilot Chat agent panel and ask for something that forces a tool call:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

Then check the server shows as running in the MCP servers view. A server that is listed but stopped is almost always a launch failure — run `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal to see the real error.

## Five questions you can ask in VS Code

Once connected, ask Copilot or Cline directly in your editor:

1. **Traffic summary**:
   ```text
   What were our top 10 landing pages by sessions over the last 30 days?
   ```
2. **Channel performance**:
   ```text
   Compare sessions, engagement rate, and bounce rate across our top 5 acquisition channels.
   ```
3. **AI search citations**:
   ```text
   How much referral traffic did we receive from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 60 days?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Analyze our traffic drop over the last 14 days compared to the prior period. Which channel fell first?
   ```
5. **E-commerce metrics**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and conversion rate by country for the past 30 days?
   ```

## Next

[Setup](/setup/) for credentials, [query shapes](/schema/) when the first query fails on a filter, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) for 35 tested templates.



# Connect ZCode Harness to Google Analytics 4 (MCP)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-zcode/


# Connect ZCode Harness to Google Analytics 4

ZCode is Z.ai's coding harness. It reads MCP servers from two possible file locations per scope, and the precedence rule between them is the thing that catches people: it is not a merge.

## Copy-paste analytical prompts

Inside ZCode session:

- **Weekly performance check**: "Compare activeUsers, sessions, and engagementRate over the last 7 days against the previous period."
- **AI referral audit**: "Show me sessions, bounceRate, and keyEvents from ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity over the last 30 days."
- **High-traffic landing pages**: "List top 10 pages by sessions and their engagementRate for the last 30 days."
- **Channel breakdown**: "Break down sessions and keyEvents by sessionDefaultChannelGroup this month."
- **Realtime visitors snapshot**: "Run a realtime report for active users and top pages over the last 30 minutes."

## The entry

In `~/.zcode/cli/config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "ga4": {
        "command": "uvx",
        "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
        "env": {
          "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
          "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Note `mcp.servers`, two levels deep. Not `mcpServers`.

## The four locations

| Scope | File | Root key |
|---|---|---|
| User | `~/.zcode/cli/config.json` | `mcp.servers` |
| Workspace | `<project>/.zcode/config.json` | `mcp.servers` |
| User, compatibility | `~/.agents/mcp.json` | `mcpServers` |
| Workspace, compatibility | `<project>/.agents/mcp.json` | `mcpServers` |

ZCode also reads the `.agents` files, which use the plain `mcpServers` shape shared with several other clients. Useful if you already maintain one, and a trap if you maintain both.

## The precedence rule

Within a single scope, `.zcode/config.json` wins **wholesale**. If it contains any server at all, the matching `.agents/mcp.json` at that scope is skipped entirely — not merged, not combined.

So a user who adds GA4 to `~/.agents/mcp.json` while `~/.zcode/cli/config.json` already holds one server sees no GA4 tools, with no error. Either consolidate into the `.zcode` file, or keep the `.agents` file as the only source at that scope.

## Legacy keys

ZCode accepts a set of older key names and translates them: `environment` is read as `env`, `http_headers` as `headers`, `enable` as `enabled`, and `type: "remote"` as `type: "http"`. The current schema takes `env`, and `type` accepts `http`, `sse` or `stdio`.

Writing `env` is the right choice for a new entry. The legacy names work, but they are compatibility rather than the current shape.

## Verify

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

If the tool list is empty, check which file ZCode actually loaded. A populated `.zcode/config.json` hides `.agents/mcp.json` at the same scope, and that is by design rather than a bug.

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [skills](/skills/) for what to load before an analytical question.



# Connect Zed Editor to Google Analytics 4 (Setup Guide)
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-mcp-for-zed/


# Connect Zed Editor to Google Analytics 4

Zed calls MCP servers **context servers**, and that is not just naming. The root key in the settings file is `context_servers`, so a snippet from any other client will not load.

## Open the settings file

From the command palette, run:

```text
zed: open settings file
```

That opens `settings.json` for Zed. Add a top-level `context_servers` key.

## The entry

```json
{
  "context_servers": {
    "google-analytics": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "GA4_PROPERTY_ID": "123456789",
        "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "/absolute/path/to/key.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

If your settings file already has content, add `context_servers` alongside it rather than replacing the file. Zed's settings hold the editor configuration and the AI configuration in the same document.

## What is different here

Three things, compared with the majority shape:

- The root key is `context_servers`, not `mcpServers`.
- There is no `type` field. Zed infers stdio from the presence of `command`.
- The file is Zed's single settings document, not a dedicated MCP file. A trailing comma anywhere in it breaks every setting, not just this one.

> **Tip:** if Zed shows no GA4 tools after saving, the settings file probably failed to parse. Zed reports a JSON error at the top of the editor for a malformed settings file, and a server that simply never appears is the symptom.

## Verify

Open the assistant panel and ask:

```text
List my GA4 properties.
```

The server appears in the context server list when it launched successfully. A listed server with no tools means the process started and exited — check `uvx google-analytics-mcp` in a terminal.

## Five questions you can ask in Zed

Once connected, ask the assistant panel directly:

1. **Top landing pages**:
   ```text
   What were our top 10 landing pages by sessions over the last 30 days?
   ```
2. **Channel performance**:
   ```text
   Compare sessions, engagement rate, and bounce rate across our acquisition channels for the past 60 days.
   ```
3. **AI referral traffic**:
   ```text
   How many sessions arrived from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity this month?
   ```
4. **Traffic change diagnosis**:
   ```text
   Diagnose why organic search traffic dropped between last week and this week. Which landing pages were most affected?
   ```
5. **E-commerce & revenue**:
   ```text
   What was our total purchase revenue and average order value (AOV) for the last 30 days grouped by country?
   ```

## Next

[Install](/setup/) for the two values, [skills](/skills/) for what to load before asking an analytical question, and [prompts](/google-analytics-ai-prompts/) for 35 tested templates.



# GA4 plugin for Claude Code
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-plugin-for-claude-code/


# GA4 plugin for Claude Code

Claude Code can install an MCP server from a plugin manifest instead of from a CLI command. The bundle ships in the repository at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`.

## What the manifest declares

```json
{
  "name": "google-analytics-mcp",
  "version": "2.11.1",
  "description": "Google Analytics 4 MCP server for real-time reporting, schema discovery, metric aggregation, and audience insights.",
  "author": { "name": "Surendran B", "url": "https://github.com/surendranb" },
  "homepage": "https://ga4.builditwithai.xyz",
  "repository": "https://github.com/surendranb/google-analytics-mcp",
  "license": "MIT",
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-analytics-mcp": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

That is the whole file. The `mcpServers` block is what Claude Code launches; everything above it is metadata.

## Plugin or plain entry

Both end up in the same place: a server named `google-analytics-mcp` launched with `uvx`. The difference is who writes it.

- A **plugin** is for distribution. Someone else adds the bundle and Claude Code reads the command from the manifest.
- A **plain entry** is for your own machine, and it can inline the two environment values so nothing prompts.

If you are setting this up once, the plain entry is fewer steps:

```bash
claude mcp add --env GA4_PROPERTY_ID=123456789 --env GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/key.json --transport stdio google-analytics -- uvx google-analytics-mcp
```

The [Claude guide](/ga4-mcp-for-claude/) covers both Claude surfaces in full.

## Version note

The plugin manifest tracks its own version number, which is not the server version. Today the manifest reads `2.11.1` while the server is on 2.11.6. The manifest version controls the bundle, not the package that `uvx` resolves — that always pulls the latest release. Read the version from the server, not from the bundle, when you need to know what is running.

## Next

[Plugins overview](/ga4-plugins/) or the [Gemini bundle](/ga4-plugin-for-gemini/).



# GA4 extension for Gemini CLI
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/ga4-plugin-for-gemini/


# GA4 extension for Gemini CLI

Gemini CLI calls these bundles extensions. The manifest lives at the repository root as `gemini-extension.json`.

## What the manifest declares

```json
{
  "name": "google-analytics-mcp",
  "version": "2.11.1",
  "description": "Google Analytics 4 MCP server for real-time reporting, schema discovery, metric aggregation, and audience insights.",
  "author": "Surendran B",
  "homepage": "https://ga4.builditwithai.xyz",
  "repository": "https://github.com/surendranb/google-analytics-mcp",
  "license": "MIT",
  "mcp": {
    "command": "uvx",
    "args": ["google-analytics-mcp"]
  },
  "settings": [
    {
      "name": "GA4_PROPERTY_ID",
      "description": "Numeric GA4 property ID (e.g. 123456789)",
      "required": true,
      "type": "string"
    },
    {
      "name": "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS",
      "description": "Path to service account JSON key file",
      "required": true,
      "type": "string"
    }
  ]
}
```

The `settings` array is the part that matters. It tells Gemini CLI to ask for both values during install, so you never open `settings.json` by hand. Both are marked `required: true`, and the extension will not finish installing without them.

## Extension or settings file

Use the extension when you want Gemini CLI to prompt for the values. Use the [settings file](/ga4-mcp-for-gemini/) when you would rather write them yourself, or when you need to set `trust` and `timeout` — the extension manifest has no equivalent for those.

## Next

[Gemini CLI guide](/ga4-mcp-for-gemini/) for the full settings shape, or [plugins overview](/ga4-plugins/).



# 35 Production GA4 Prompts for Claude, Cursor & AI
URL: https://ga4mcp.com/google-analytics-ai-prompts/


# 35 Production GA4 Prompts for Claude, Cursor & AI Agents

Querying Google Analytics 4 through an AI agent requires prompts that instruct the model on methodology, comparison periods, and scope. Vague questions like *"How is my site doing?"* produce vague summaries. Precise prompts produce actionable analytical breakdowns.

This cookbook provides 35 tested prompts designed for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and any MCP-compatible client connected to GA4 MCP.

## 1. Traffic Change & Drop Diagnosis

Use these prompts when metrics shift unexpectedly and you need to isolate the root cause before reacting.

### Prompt 1.1: Sudden Traffic Drop Triage
```text
Diagnose our traffic over the last 14 days compared to the prior 14-day period. 
Break down sessions, active users, and engagement rate by sessionDefaultChannelGroup. 
Identify which specific channel drove the decline and check if the drop was site-wide or isolated to specific landing pages.
```
*API calls: `get_ga4_data` with `sessionDefaultChannelGroup`, `date`, `sessions`, `activeUsers`, `engagementRate`.*

### Prompt 1.2: Organic Search Drop vs. Tracking Snippet Error
```text
Our organic traffic dropped this week. Compare the last 7 days to the previous 7 days. 
Check daily session totals alongside landingPage paths. 
Tell me if the drop occurred as a sudden cliff (suggesting a broken tag or consent banner) or a gradual slide (suggesting a ranking or algorithm change).
```

### Prompt 1.3: Direct Traffic Spike Audit
```text
We had an unexpected spike in direct traffic over the last 48 hours. 
Pull sessions, screenPageViews, and userEngagementDuration broken down by city and deviceCategory. 
Check whether this traffic exhibits bot patterns (near-zero engagement duration, 100% single-page views, single datacenter origin).
```

### Prompt 1.4: Channel Mix Shift
```text
Analyze our traffic mix over the last 30 days compared to the 30 days before that. 
Calculate the percentage share of total sessions for each sessionDefaultChannelGroup. 
Which channels gained share and which channels lost share?
```

### Prompt 1.5: Weekend vs. Weekday Traffic Baseline
```text
Pull our daily sessions and active users for the past 6 weeks. 
Calculate our average weekday volume versus our average weekend volume. 
Flag any weekday that fell more than 20% below our trailing weekday average.
```

### Prompt 1.6: Campaign UTM Performance Audit
```text
List all sessions from the past 30 days where sessionMedium is 'cpc' or 'paid'. 
Group by sessionCampaign and sessionSource. 
Report sessions, keyEvents, and engagementRate to identify our best-performing and lowest-performing paid campaigns.
```

---

## 2. AI Search & Answer Engine Tracking

Measure visitors arriving from generative AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini).

### Prompt 2.1: Monthly AI Referral Overview
```text
Identify all referral traffic from AI platforms over the last 90 days. 
Filter sessionSource for chatgpt.com, chat.openai.com, claude.ai, perplexity.ai, and gemini.google.com. 
Report monthly sessions, activeUsers, and average engagement duration per source.
```

### Prompt 2.2: AI Traffic Quality vs. Organic Search
```text
Compare the engagement quality of AI assistant referrals (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude) against traditional Organic Search for the last 30 days. 
Show sessions, bounceRate, userEngagementDuration, and keyEvents per session.
```

### Prompt 2.3: Top Landing Pages for AI Visitors
```text
Which specific landing pages are AI assistants citing? 
Filter sessionSource for chatgpt.com and perplexity.ai over the last 60 days. 
List landingPage sorted by sessions descending with total pageviews and key events.
```

### Prompt 2.4: Perplexity vs. ChatGPT Share
```text
Calculate the traffic split between ChatGPT (chatgpt.com, chat.openai.com) and Perplexity (perplexity.ai) over the last 30 days. 
Show daily session trends for both sources to determine which assistant is growing faster on our domain.
```

### Prompt 2.5: Conversion Rate of AI Referrals
```text
What is the key event conversion rate for visitors arriving from AI assistants compared to our site-wide average? 
Pull sessions and keyEvents for AI sources over the last 90 days and calculate keyEvents per session.
```

### Prompt 2.6: New User Acquisition via AI Engines
```text
How many first-time visitors arrived via AI engines this quarter? 
Query newUsers and sessions where sessionSource matches AI platforms, and calculate new users as a percentage of total AI sessions.
```

---

## 3. Acquisition & Channel Performance

Evaluate how marketing channels deliver qualified visitors.

### Prompt 3.1: Top Acquisition Channels Overview
```text
Summarize our top 10 acquisition channels for the past 30 days. 
Include sessions, activeUsers, screenPageViewsPerSession, averageSessionDuration, and keyEvents. 
Sort by sessions descending.
```

### Prompt 3.2: First User vs. Session Channel Comparison
```text
Compare firstUserDefaultChannelGroup (how users first discovered us) with sessionDefaultChannelGroup (how users returned) for the last 60 days. 
Highlight channels that drive discovery versus channels that drive return visits.
```

### Prompt 3.3: Referral Domain Quality Breakdown
```text
List the top 15 referring websites (sessionSource where sessionMedium is 'referral') over the last 30 days. 
Report sessions, engagementRate, and keyEvents. Exclude internal subdomains.
```

### Prompt 3.4: Social Media Channel Comparison
```text
Break down traffic from social media platforms over the last 30 days. 
Filter for sessionDefaultChannelGroup equals 'Organic Social' and 'Paid Social'. 
Compare LinkedIn, Twitter/X, YouTube, and Reddit by engagement rate and key events.
```

### Prompt 3.5: Email Campaign ROI
```text
Pull all traffic where sessionMedium equals 'email' for the past 60 days. 
Group by sessionCampaign and show sessions, userEngagementDuration, and keyEvents to identify our most effective newsletter sends.
```

### Prompt 3.6: Unassigned Traffic Diagnosis
```text
Check how much traffic fell into the 'Unassigned' channel group over the last 30 days. 
Pull sessionSource and sessionMedium for all Unassigned sessions so we can identify broken UTM parameters.
```

---

## 4. Content & Landing Page Audits

Discover which URLs attract visitors and which lose them immediately.

### Prompt 4.1: Top 20 Landing Pages by Engagement
```text
List our top 20 landing pages by organic search traffic over the last 30 days. 
Report sessions, activeUsers, userEngagementDuration, and bounceRate. 
Sort by userEngagementDuration descending.
```

### Prompt 4.2: High-Traffic, High-Bounce Page Alert
```text
Find all landing pages that received at least 250 sessions over the past 30 days but have a bounce rate above 65%. 
Sort by session volume descending so we know which pages require immediate UX or content revision.
```

### Prompt 4.3: New Content Velocity Check
```text
Audit traffic to all URLs under our blog or docs path published in the last 60 days. 
Show weekly screenPageViews and active users for each URL since publication.
```

### Prompt 4.4: Low-Performing Content Audit
```text
Identify pages on our site that received fewer than 20 total screenPageViews over the past 90 days. 
Group by pagePath and sort ascending to help us plan content pruning or consolidation.
```

### Prompt 4.5: Internal Search Terms Analysis
```text
What terms are visitors searching for inside our site? 
Query the searchTerm dimension for the last 30 days with eventCount and activeUsers. 
Sort by frequency descending.
```

### Prompt 4.6: Desktop vs. Mobile Landing Page Drop-off
```text
Compare bounceRate and userEngagementDuration across mobile and desktop for our top 10 landing pages over the last 30 days. 
Flag pages where mobile bounce rate exceeds desktop bounce rate by more than 15 percentage points.
```

---

## 5. E-Commerce & Funnel Conversion

Analyze purchases, average order value, and checkout drop-offs.

### Prompt 5.1: Overall E-Commerce Performance Summary
```text
Summarize our e-commerce performance for the last 30 days compared to the prior 30 days. 
Report purchaseRevenue, transactions, averagePurchaseRevenue, and ecommercePurchases. 
Calculate our average order value (AOV).
```

### Prompt 5.2: Revenue by Acquisition Channel
```text
Which marketing channels generate the most revenue? 
Break down purchaseRevenue, transactions, and averagePurchaseRevenue by sessionDefaultChannelGroup for the last 60 days. 
Sort by purchaseRevenue descending.
```

### Prompt 5.3: Checkout Funnel Drop-off Analysis
```text
Examine our checkout funnel events over the last 30 days: view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, and purchase. 
Report the total eventCount for each stage and calculate the drop-off percentage between each consecutive step.
```

### Prompt 5.4: Top 15 Products by Revenue
```text
List our top 15 products by gross revenue over the past 90 days. 
Query itemName, itemRevenue, itemsPurchased, and itemsViewed. 
Calculate the view-to-purchase conversion rate for each product.
```

### Prompt 5.5: High Cart-Abandonment Products
```text
Identify products with high cart additions but low final purchases over the last 60 days. 
Compare itemsAddedToCart against itemsPurchased per itemName for all items added to cart at least 50 times.
```

### Prompt 5.6: Repeat Buyer vs. First-Time Buyer Revenue
```text
Compare revenue generated by new users versus returning users over the last 60 days. 
Query newUsers and activeUsers alongside purchaseRevenue grouped by newVsReturning dimension.
```

---

## 6. Geographic, Device & Audience Segmentation

Identify international opportunities and hardware friction.

### Prompt 6.1: Top Countries by Active Users & Value
```text
List our top 15 countries by activeUsers over the last 30 days. 
Show sessions, userEngagementDuration, and keyEvents per country. 
Sort by activeUsers descending.
```

### Prompt 6.2: City-Level Growth in Primary Market
```text
Filter traffic to our primary country over the last 60 days. 
Break down sessions, activeUsers, and keyEvents by city. 
Identify the top 10 fastest-growing metropolitan areas.
```

### Prompt 6.3: Browser & Operating System Health Check
```text
Audit traffic by browser and operatingSystem for the past 30 days. 
Check bounceRate and engagementRate across Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge, and mobile in-app browsers. 
Flag any browser with an unusually high bounce rate that might indicate a rendering bug.
```

### Prompt 6.4: Screen Resolution Friction Analysis
```text
Pull screenResolution with sessions and bounceRate for mobile devices over the last 30 days. 
Check whether specific small-screen resolutions suffer from higher drop-off rates.
```

### Prompt 6.5: New vs. Returning User Engagement
```text
Compare new users and returning users over the last 90 days. 
Report sessions, userEngagementDuration, screenPageViewsPerSession, and keyEvents to see how customer retention influences overall engagement.
```

---
